title: The rainbow (Genesis 9:8–17)
hook: God's first covenant is with all living things, and the bow in the cloud is its sign

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dove and the olive leaf, freshly plucked, the first sign the flood was easing. Your line was the leaf comes back. Did you spot one? Day thirty-five.

The door of the ark opens. Out come Noah, his wife, his sons and their wives, and then the animals, blinking, into a washed-out world. The ground is mud. Everything they knew is gone. And the first thing God does is make a promise. Not only to Noah. The Torah is almost fussy about the guest list: to you, and to your children after you, and to every living creature that is with you, the fowl, the cattle, every beast of the earth. Never again, God says, will a flood destroy the earth. And then God points at the sky after the rain, at something every child has stopped to stare at. Today's word is the promise.
screen: `THE DOOR OPENS ONTO MUD.` → `A PROMISE WITH A GUEST LIST.` → `EVERY LIVING CREATURE.`

segments.voice: Brit. A covenant: a binding promise between two sides. It's one of the biggest words in Jewish life. A baby boy's circumcision is called a brit milah, the covenant of circumcision. Sinai will be a brit. But here's what's striking. The first brit in the Torah isn't with Abraham, and it isn't with Israel. It's with everyone. Every person, every animal, the whole earth. In the old JPS translation: "I have set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between Me and the earth." The word for the bow is keshet. It's the ordinary Hebrew word for a rainbow, and also for a bow, the weapon. Some commentators noticed that a rainbow looks like a bow with its ends pointing down toward the ground, aimed away from the earth: a weapon hung up in the sky. And the rabbis built something lasting on this covenant. They taught that all people, the children of Noah, are bound by seven basic laws, among them not to murder, not to steal, and to set up courts of justice. Jewish tradition holds that anyone who lives by these is righteous, whatever their people. And there's a blessing, from the Talmud, that many Jews say when they see a rainbow: it praises God who remembers the covenant and keeps the promise. Think about that. A rainbow is a promise God made to every living thing, and people stop in parking lots to look at it. It's a promise to everything.
screen: `BRIT — A BINDING PROMISE.` · `THE FIRST COVENANT IS WITH ALL.` · `KESHET — A BOW HUNG UP.` · `THE SEVEN LAWS OF NOAH.` · then, large: `A TOKEN OF A COVENANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of a promise you could actually keep. Not a big vow. Something small: I'll call my mother on Sunday. I'll put my phone away at dinner. I'll feed the birds this week. Say it to yourself, quietly, and picture keeping it. If you pray, you can offer it in your prayer. If not, just let it settle. A covenant starts with one promise kept. The bell holds the time.
Brit. A covenant, and the first one is with every living thing. That ends the fifth week: clothes for the road, Cain and Abel, my brother's keeper, tzaddik, the ark, the dove, and brit.
Your line: a promise to everything. Today, make that one small promise, and keep it before the day ends. Day thirty-five.

howItsDone: Many Jews say a short blessing from the Talmud on seeing a rainbow, praising God who remembers the covenant; the idea of the seven Noahide laws for all humanity comes from this covenant with Noah.

fork.setup: the flood is over and God makes the first covenant. who is it with?
options: Noah, his children, and every living creature.
fork.reveal: every living creature: birds, cattle, every beast. the first brit in the Torah includes the whole earth.

original.note: Hebrew: a covenant, a binding promise between two sides.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rainbow is a pretty sign after rain.
what it means: the sign of the first brit, God's promise to every living creature never again to destroy the earth by flood.
what a scholar hears: keshet, also a war bow. and Sanhedrin 56a, where the rabbis draw the seven Noahide laws for all people from this covenant.

sources.quoted: I have set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between Me and the earth.

notes: The bow-pointing-away reading is usually attributed to Ramban on Genesis 9:12 (bow's ends turned down away from the earth / not aimed at it). Confirm the direction described and attribution; the script says only 'some commentators'.

Seven Noahide laws (Sanhedrin 56a) and 'the righteous of the nations' idea (Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2; Maimonides, Laws of Kings 8:11): the script says anyone who lives by these is righteous. Confirm that this wording is acceptable across movements.
Week 5 look-back lists days 29–35: confirm day 29's title 'clothes for the road' is the right name to recall.
